input.strategy_title: Audit logging for model inference traffic
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Financial-services customers cannot pass compliance reviews because inference
traffic on RHOAI leaves no audit trail: there is no record of who invoked which
model endpoint, when, and with what outcome. Auditors require tamper-evident,
structured audit events for every inference request. Without this, two
strategic renewals are at risk this fiscal year.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | Every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an audit event capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status (not payloads). |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Audit events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with at-least-once semantics and are not lost on component restart. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | Administrators can enable/disable inference auditing per project from the Dashboard. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | A common audit event schema is defined and published so future components (pipelines, workbenches) emit compatible events. Note: the schema in this item is the format HLR-1's events must conform to — HLR-1 cannot ship before the schema is settled. |
| HLR-5 | P2 | Documentation covers enabling auditing and interpreting events. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Dashboard

## Out of Scope

- Auditing of non-inference traffic (pipeline runs, notebook activity) — future
  strategies will adopt the HLR-4 schema
- Long-term audit storage and retention tooling (customer-provided)

## Open Questions

None — the audit sink interface is the standard cluster logging forwarder.

# Define and publish the common inference audit event schema

## Description

This epic delivers the common audit event schema for model inference
traffic: a versioned, published definition of the structured audit event
that inference components emit. The schema captures caller identity,
model/version, timestamp, and response status, and explicitly excludes
request/response payloads. It is the contract that inference audit event
emission conforms to and that future components (pipelines, workbenches)
will adopt in later strategies, so it must be component-agnostic rather than
specific to any single emitter.

## Scope

- Define the audit event schema: fields for caller identity, model and
  model version, timestamp, and response status (success/failure outcome).
- State explicitly in the schema that request and response payloads are not
  captured, so emitters and auditors have an unambiguous data-minimization
  contract.
- Version the schema so future components can emit compatible events and
  evolution is possible without breaking consumers.
- Publish the schema at a location accessible to platform components and
  auditors, suitable for adoption by future strategies (pipelines,
  workbenches are out of scope for this strategy but named as adopters).
- Align the delivery target semantics with the cluster audit sink (the
  standard cluster logging forwarder interface) so events defined by this
  schema can be forwarded without translation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The schema document exists and defines fields covering caller identity,
  model/version, timestamp, and response status.
- The schema states that payloads are excluded from audit events.
- The schema carries a version identifier and a documented compatibility
  expectation for future emitting components.
- The schema is published at an agreed, discoverable location reachable by
  platform components and by consumers of the cluster audit sink.
- The schema has been reviewed for component-agnosticism: nothing in it
  presumes a single emitter's internal structure.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): A common audit event schema is defined and published so
  future components emit compatible events. This epic also produces the
  format that the P0 inference audit events (HLR-1) must conform to, which
  is why this epic is prioritized P0 despite HLR-4's P2 label.

# KServe inference audit event emission and at-least-once delivery

## Description

This epic delivers inference audit logging in the KServe serving stack:
every inference request processed through a KServe endpoint emits a
structured audit event conforming to the published common audit event
schema, and events are delivered to the cluster audit sink (the standard
cluster logging forwarder interface) with at-least-once semantics that
survive component restarts. It also implements the serving-side honoring of
the per-project inference auditing enablement setting that the Dashboard
control writes.

## Scope

- Emit one audit event per inference request handled by a KServe endpoint,
  capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and response status,
  and never capturing request or response payloads.
- Emit events that conform to the published common inference audit event
  schema.
- Deliver events to the cluster audit sink via the standard cluster logging
  forwarder interface with at-least-once semantics.
- Ensure no audit events are lost when a serving component restarts
  (durable buffering or an equivalent mechanism in the delivery path, sized
  and bounded during implementation).
- Honor a per-project inference auditing enablement setting: audit event
  emission for a project's inference endpoints is gated by that project's
  setting, so administrators can enable/disable auditing per project.
- Cover all inference traffic through KServe endpoints in both deployment
  modes supported by the serving stack (serverless and raw deployment).

## Acceptance Criteria

- For a sample of inference requests through a KServe endpoint, each
  request produces exactly one audit event containing caller identity,
  model/version, timestamp, and response status, and containing no request
  or response payload data.
- Emitted events validate against the published common audit event schema.
- With the cluster logging forwarder configured as audit sink, events
  arrive at the sink at least once per emitted event.
- Restarting the serving component during active inference traffic does not
  result in loss of audit events for requests processed before the restart.
- With per-project auditing disabled for a project, inference requests to
  that project's endpoints produce no audit events; with it enabled, they
  produce events per the criteria above.
- The change is covered by the existing build pipeline for the serving
  stack (pipeline green on the merged change).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): Every inference request through a KServe endpoint emits an
  audit event capturing caller identity, model/version, timestamp, and
  response status (not payloads).
- HLR-2 (P0): Audit events are delivered to the cluster audit sink with
  at-least-once semantics and are not lost on component restart.
- HLR-3 (P1, serving-side scope only): the per-project enablement setting
  honored here is the configuration surface that the Dashboard control
  writes; the user-facing Dashboard surface is tracked separately.

# Dashboard per-project control for inference auditing

## Description

This epic delivers the administrator-facing control in the RHOAI Dashboard
that enables and disables inference auditing per data science project.
Administrators use this control to turn audit event emission on or off for
a project's inference endpoints; the setting is the per-project inference
auditing configuration that the serving stack honors when emitting audit
events.

## Scope

- Add a per-project inference auditing enable/disable control to the
  Dashboard, following the Dashboard's existing patterns for per-project
  and per-component settings (the Dashboard reads and writes Kubernetes
  CRs and owns no data plane).
- Write the per-project audit enablement configuration that the
  serving-side inference auditing implementation consumes, using the
  configuration surface defined by that implementation.
- Reflect the current effective state of the per-project auditing setting
  in the control (round-trip: change the setting, reload, state persists).
- Restrict the control to administrator-level access consistent with the
  Dashboard's existing project-scoped RBAC behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An administrator can enable and disable inference auditing for a project
  from the Dashboard, and the chosen state persists and is displayed
  correctly on reload.
- The control writes the per-project inference auditing configuration that
  the serving stack honors — toggling the control changes whether audit
  events are emitted for that project's inference endpoints.
- The control is visible and mutable only to users with the intended
  administrator-level access; non-administrator project users cannot change
  it.
- The change is covered by the existing Dashboard build pipeline (pipeline
  green on the merged change).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): Administrators can enable/disable inference auditing per
  project from the Dashboard.

# Document enabling inference auditing and interpreting audit events

## Description

This epic delivers the end-user documentation for inference audit logging:
how administrators enable and disable inference auditing (including the
per-project Dashboard control), where audit events are delivered (the
cluster audit sink via the standard cluster logging forwarder), and how to
interpret the fields of an audit event against the published common audit
event schema.

## Scope

- New documentation topic covering:
  - What inference auditing captures (caller identity, model/version,
    timestamp, response status) and what it deliberately does not capture
    (payloads).
  - How to enable and disable inference auditing per project from the
    Dashboard, including the administrator access required.
  - Where audit events are delivered (cluster audit sink / cluster logging
    forwarder) and any prerequisites on the customer side (long-term
    storage and retention are customer-provided and out of scope for the
    product, per the strategy).
  - How to interpret audit events: field-by-field reference against the
    published common audit event schema and its version.
  - At-least-once delivery semantics and what restart-survivability means
    for audit completeness, so auditors understand the guarantee.
- Follow the Red Hat docs content process and toolchain for authoring and
  publishing the topic.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A published documentation topic exists covering enabling/disabling
  inference auditing per project and interpreting inference audit events.
- The topic's field reference matches the published common audit event
  schema (correct fields, correct payload-exclusion statement, correct
  schema version).
- The documented enable/disable procedure matches the actual Dashboard
  control and the serving-side behavior.
- The documentation has been technically reviewed against the implemented
  behavior by someone from the implementing teams before publication.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P2): Documentation covers enabling auditing and interpreting
  events.

# Decomposition Summary — RHAISTRAT-9010 (Audit logging for model inference traffic)

Strategy status: Refinement Done, priority Critical. The strategy defines
inference audit event emission in KServe, reliable delivery to the cluster
audit sink, a per-project on/off control in the Dashboard, a published common
audit event schema, and end-user documentation.

**Triage:** Not below-threshold and not docs-only. Although the strategy is
small, it spans multiple architecturally distinct work streams (serving-side
event emission and delivery pipeline, Dashboard UI control surface, and
substantive documentation authoring) that warrant separate PR review cycles
and different skills. Full decomposition follows.

**Staff Engineer Input:** none present in the strategy.

## Step 1 — Strategy structure

The strategy provides: High-Level Requirements (HLR-1..HLR-5 with
priorities), Affected Components (KServe, Dashboard), Out of Scope, and Open
Questions ("None — the audit sink interface is the standard cluster logging
forwarder"). Health warnings for missing sections are listed below.

## Step 2 — Component graph

| Component (canonical) | Change | Owner team | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|
| KServe | Emit audit events per inference request, deliver to cluster audit sink, honor per-project enablement | RHOAI Serving | Active |
| Dashboard | Administrator per-project enable/disable control for inference auditing | RHOAI Dashboard | Active |
| Documentation | New documentation topic: enabling auditing and interpreting events | RHOAI Documentation | Active (docs-authoring) |

Both KServe and Dashboard exist in `.context/architecture-context/`
(rhoai-3.0) and are Konflux-onboarded — no onboarding chain (Rule 20) is
needed. No new components are provisioned.

Component mapping notes:
- The common audit event schema epic is assigned canonical component
  `KServe` (single most-relevant name): the schema is authored by the
  serving team whose component emits the first conforming events, and there
  is no canonical "platform-wide schema" component. The deliverable is
  explicitly component-agnostic per HLR-4.
- HLR-5 requires documentation, but `Documentation` is not listed in the
  strategy's Affected Components. It is added as an epic under the canonical
  `Documentation` component.

## Step 3 — Investigations

The strategy declares no open questions, no pending reviews, and no
conditional ADRs; the audit sink interface is stated to be the standard
cluster logging forwarder. No unknown changes which epics exist or what they
do. The only sequencing constraint (HLR-4's note that HLR-1 cannot ship
before the schema is settled) is a build-against artifact relationship
(Rule 13), not an uncertainty — it is modeled as a dependency edge, not an
Investigation. The strategy is compliance-driven but is not a
guardrails/sandboxing/RBAC enforcement strategy (Rule 19 does not trigger).

## Step 4 — HLR-to-epic mapping

- HLR-1 (P0) and HLR-2 (P0) both describe the KServe audit event pipeline —
  emission at the inference endpoint and reliable at-least-once delivery of
  those same events. Same component, same team, same logical change over the
  same event stream: one Implementation epic covering both HLRs at P0.
- HLR-3 (P1) is a distinct, deferrable feature on a different component and
  UI surface (Dashboard per-project control): separate epic at P1.
- HLR-4 (P2) is the published common audit event schema. It is a distinct
  deliverable (a published contract for future components) that HLR-1's
  events must conform to, so it is its own epic. Because it transitively
  gates all P0 work (HLR-1/HLR-2), it inherits P0 (priority inheritance).
- HLR-5 (P2) is substantive documentation authoring (new doc topic), a
  separate work-product type: separate `docs-authoring` epic. Per the
  docs-authoring priority exception, its priority derives from the strategy
  frontmatter priority (Critical → P0), and its edges do not trigger

| RHAISTRAT-9010-E002 | KServe inference audit event emission and at-least-once delivery | Implementation | RHOAI Serving | P0 |

- **Missing strategy sections (non-blocking):** no Impacted Teams table, no

  decomposition by priority inheritance: the schema epic (E001) is P0.

  restart" plus at-least-once semantics implies durable buffering in the

  (pipelines, workbenches) but is being defined under the KServe component

  component-agnostic and its publication location is agreed platform-wide.
- **Documentation component absent from Affected Components:** HLR-5
  requires documentation; the strategy lists only KServe and Dashboard. A
  Documentation epic was added — confirm the intended docs owner.

## Tiered Delivery

Not applicable — no external dependency with uncertain timing; all work is
in-platform and linearly gated by the schema.
